title: Hummingbirds
objective: After this level you can describe hummingbirds' speed and energy needs.
summary: A flying ruby-throated hummingbird's heart tops 1,200 beats a minute, and hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for long. Tiny and poorly insulated, they save energy at night in torpor.

cards.headline: A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,200 times a minute.
cards.body: That's a ruby-throated hummingbird in flight, according to the Smithsonian's National Zoo. At rest it drops to about 225. A human athlete working hard reaches only about 150. What kind of life needs an engine like that?

cards.headline: The only true hoverers
cards.body: Hummingbirds are the only vertebrates that can hover for a sustained time, parked in midair in front of a flower. They can fly backward, and even upside down. A ruby-throated hummingbird beats its wings about 70 times a second in ordinary flight, and more than 200 times a second in a dive. That's a lot of flapping just to stand still.

cards.headline: A tiny furnace with a thin coat
cards.body: Hummingbirds weigh just 2 to 20 grams, their feathers are poor insulation, and their metabolic demands are enormous. Remember Level 5: making your own heat costs food, which is why a lizard can eat so much less than a warm-blooded animal its size. A hummingbird is the extreme case, a tiny bird with a thin coat and a racing engine.

cards.fact: At night, a hummingbird can nearly switch itself off.
cards.context: When a night is cold or food is short, a hummingbird can drop into torpor: a deep, sleep-like state with its metabolism slowed to a minimum and its body temperature very low. In a study published in 2020, a black metaltail hummingbird in the Peruvian Andes cooled to 3.3 °C, the lowest body temperature recorded for any bird or non-hibernating mammal.

mascot.line: Hold on to torpor. Level 64 brings it back for a whole winter.

cards.headline: Hummingbirds: explained
learned: Heart: about 225 at rest, over 1,200 in flight
The only vertebrates that hover for long
Tiny, poorly insulated, huge energy needs
Torpor saves energy; one cooled to 3.3 °C

questions.prompt: About how fast can a flying ruby-throated hummingbird's heart beat?

options.label: About 150 beats a minute
options.rationale: That's a human athlete working hard.

questions.explanation: A ruby-throated hummingbird's heart runs from about 225 at rest to more than 1,200 beats a minute in flight.

questions.prompt: Why does a hummingbird drop into torpor on a cold night?

options.label: To slow its body down and save energy
To digest a big meal of nectar
options.rationale: Torpor slows everything down, digestion included.

options.label: To hide from owls by staying still
options.rationale: The card is about energy, not hiding.

questions.explanation: In torpor a hummingbird slows its metabolism to a minimum and lets its body temperature fall, saving energy.

questions.prompt: Level 5 said making your own heat costs food. Why does that bill hit hummingbirds so hard?

options.label: They are ectotherms that must bask
options.rationale: They are birds, which make their own heat.

options.label: They eat only once a day
options.rationale: The card doesn't say so; the issue is their tiny, costly bodies.

options.label: They're tiny, poorly insulated, and burn energy fast
They fly only in the tropics
options.rationale: The issue is their bodies, not where they live.

questions.explanation: At 2 to 20 grams, with poor insulation and huge metabolic demands, hummingbirds pay the heat bill hardest.
